snapshot.title: UPSC Environment: Protected Areas & Species-in-News
snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ UPSC v12.0 Hook: Kuno: Cheetah. Dugong: Sea Cow. Gahirmatha: Turtles. Sangai: Manipur. 75: Ramsar.

quick_notes.title: Species in News (Recent)
quick_notes.detail: Cheetah (Kuno NP, Project Cheetah). Great Indian Bustard (Critically Endangered, Great Indian Bustard project). Sangai Deer (Phumdis, Keibul Lamjao).
quick_notes.explanation: The cheetah is a large wild cat that was extinct in India for decades, and it has been reintroduced to Kuno National Park (NP) in Madhya Pradesh under Project Cheetah, which is a government effort to bring the species back. The Great Indian Bustard is a large, heavy bird found in grasslands, and it is listed as Critically Endangered, meaning it faces an extremely high risk of extinction in the wild, so the Great Indian Bustard project works to protect its remaining population. The Sangai deer is a rare, brow-antlered deer that lives only on floating mats of vegetation called phumdis in Loktak Lake, and it is protected in Keibul Lamjao National Park in Manipur, which is the world's only floating national park.

quick_notes.title: Marine Species
quick_notes.detail: Dugong (Sea Cow - Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay). Olive Ridley Turtles (Gahirmatha, Arribada). Ganges River Dolphin (National Aquatic Animal).
quick_notes.explanation: Marine Species are animals that live in oceans or rivers connected to the sea. The Dugong, also called a Sea Cow, is a large marine mammal that eats seagrass and is found in the Gulf of Mannar and Palk Bay, which are coastal areas between India and Sri Lanka. Olive Ridley Turtles are a type of sea turtle famous for a mass nesting event called Arribada, where thousands of females come ashore together to lay eggs, and the main nesting site in India is Gahirmatha beach in Odisha. The Ganges River Dolphin is a freshwater dolphin that lives in the Ganges and Brahmaputra river systems, and it has been declared the National Aquatic Animal of India.

quick_notes.title: IUCN Status Recap
quick_notes.detail: CR (Critically Endangered), EN (Endangered), VU (Vulnerable). Snow Leopard (VU). Asiatic Lion (Endangered).
quick_notes.explanation: The IUCN, or International Union for Conservation of Nature, is a global organization that creates a list, called the Red List, to show how close a species is to dying out completely. The list uses categories to describe a species' risk of extinction, and the three highest risk categories are Critically Endangered (CR), Endangered (EN), and Vulnerable (VU). A species listed as Critically Endangered (CR) faces an extremely high risk of extinction in the wild, while Endangered (EN) means it faces a very high risk, and Vulnerable (VU) means it faces a high risk. For example, the Snow Leopard is listed as Vulnerable (VU), meaning it is at high risk of extinction but not as high as an Endangered species. The Asiatic Lion is listed as Endangered (EN), meaning it faces a very high risk of extinction in the wild.

quick_notes.title: Ramsar Sites (75+)
quick_notes.detail: Chilika (1st site). Wular (Freshwater). Sambhar (Saline). Renuka (Smallest). Sundarbans (Largest).
quick_notes.explanation: Ramsar Sites are wetlands—areas of marsh, pond, or coast—that are internationally recognized as important for the world’s water birds and other wildlife under the Ramsar Convention, which is a global treaty signed in 1971 to protect these habitats. India has named over 75 such sites. The first Ramsar Site in India was Chilika Lake, a large brackish (slightly salty) lagoon on the east coast famous for migratory birds. Wular Lake, in Jammu and Kashmir, is India’s largest freshwater lake—water with very little salt—and it is a Ramsar Site. Sambhar Lake, in Rajasthan, is a saline (salty) inland lake and the country’s largest saltwater lake designated as a Ramsar Site. Renuka Lake, in Himachal Pradesh, is the smallest Ramsar Site in India by area, while the Sundarbans, the vast mangrove forest straddling India and Bangladesh, is the largest Ramsar Site in India by area.

quick_notes.title: Forest Types
quick_notes.detail: Tropical Evergreen (Western Ghats). Tropical Deciduous (Most widespread in India). Mangroves (Sundarbans, Bhitarkanika).
quick_notes.explanation: Forests in India are classified into different types based on the climate and rainfall they receive. Tropical Evergreen forests are found in areas with very heavy rainfall, like the Western Ghats, and they stay green all year because the trees never shed all their leaves at once. Tropical Deciduous forests are the most widespread type in India; they lose their leaves during the dry season to save water. Mangroves are special forests that grow in salty, muddy coastal areas, and the largest mangrove forest in the world is the Sundarbans, located in West Bengal, with another important one called Bhitarkanika in Odisha.
